title: Central air conditioner or heat pump (outdoor unit): safe teardown
summary: The outdoor unit gives a 208/230 V fan motor and its big propeller blade, a 24 V contactor, a dual run capacitor, the disconnect with its fuses, sensors and galvanised steel panels. It is fed by two circuits and its capacitor (rated 440 V on the Goodman) can stay charged after the power is off, so switch off and tag both, then discharge and prove dead. The compressor and coil hold kilograms of refrigerant under pressure: leave them sealed.

steps.text: Read the rating plate on the side of the cabinet: volts, refrigerant (R-22 on older units, R-410A on later ones, and a flammable one such as R-454B on the newest) and its charge. Look for cut or crushed copper lines, oily stains or a smashed coil, and decide which parts you want.
steps.warn: A cut line set doesn't prove the outdoor unit is empty: closed service valves can hold the whole charge inside. Treat every unit as charged. Hissing, oily stains or frost on a broken line mean a leak: step back, keep flames and sparks away and read safety_refrigerant.

steps.text: Switch off the unit's two-pole breaker in the house panel, then the outdoor disconnect on the wall beside the unit (pull the block out, or turn the switch off). Tape or lock both off with a note: Working on this. Do not switch on.
steps.warn: Carrier warns there may be more than one disconnect. Pulling the block only kills the unit's side: the supply terminals inside the box stay live until the panel breaker is off.

steps.text: Switch off the indoor furnace or air handler at its service switch and its breaker, and tag both. It supplies the 24 V control power that tells the outdoor unit to run.
steps.warn: Don't rely on the thermostat being off: it only switches the 24 V control wires, never the outdoor unit's 240 V supply.

steps.text: Find any other source that could feed the building: a generator, a solar or battery inverter, or a changeover switch. Switch it off at the source and tag it (see safety_mains_isolation). Then wait 5 minutes.
steps.warn: A generator or inverter wired into the building can make the panel live with the grid down.

steps.text: Take off the control-box access panel (a few screws on one corner panel) and look without touching. Find the dual run capacitor (a round or oval can with terminals usually marked C, HERM and FAN), any extra start capacitor and relay from a hard-start kit, and the contactor. If you find a large circuit board with big cylindrical capacitors instead of a simple contactor (an inverter or variable-speed drive), don't touch it: read the motor-drive section of safety_discharge_capacitor first, and if you can't find the DC bus or it reads over 1,000 V, close the cover and leave the unit.
steps.warn: Wear gloves and safety glasses: the sheet metal has sharp edges and burrs. If the unit ran recently, the compressor dome may still be hot.

steps.text: Discharge the run capacitor with your resistor tool. Clip the lead to C and hold the probe on HERM, then on FAN, for at least 10 seconds each. Then clip the lead to bare cabinet metal and touch each terminal in turn. Do the same to any start capacitor (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: Never short it with a screwdriver: many motor capacitors are internally fused and shorting can ruin them. Friedrich says that on a 230 V circuit a motor's start terminal can reach as high as 400 V while running: treat the capacitor as live until the meter reads under 1 V.

steps.text: Prove it dead. Check your meter on a known live source. On AC volts, measure between the two incoming supply wires at the contactor's line side and from each to the earth lug. On DC volts, measure C to HERM, C to FAN and each terminal to the cabinet. Everything must read under 1 V. Check the meter on the known source again, then clip a jumper wire across the capacitor terminals.
steps.warn: If anything reads live, stop and find the supply you missed. A one-pole contactor (Goodman lists one) can leave one supply leg wired straight to the compressor and fan, and a crankcase heater can be powered while the unit sits silent.

steps.text: Photograph the wiring and put a tape label on every wire before you undo anything.

Take the controls: the run capacitor (undo its strap and pull the spade connectors), the contactor (usually two screws), any hard-start capacitor and relay, and on a heat pump the defrost control board. Twist a bare wire across each capacitor's terminals before you store it.
Trace the fan motor's leads from the control box up to the top of the cabinet and free them from their clips and grommets, so the top can lift off without dragging them.

Undo the screws around the top panel or fan grille. If the fan motor is bolted under the grille, the grille, motor and blade lift off as one piece; if it sits on a bracket, unbolt the bracket instead. Lift it with a helper and set it upside down on cardboard.
steps.warn: The top with its motor and blade is heavy and awkward. Keep fingers out from under it and clear of the blade edges.

steps.text: Loosen the set screw on the blade's hub and slide the blade off the shaft; soak a rusted hub in penetrating oil and wait, or use a puller. Then undo the nuts holding the motor and lift it off.
steps.warn: Don't hammer the end of the shaft: it damages the motor's bearings.

steps.text: Unclip any temperature sensor clipped onto a tube, and leave everything else on the refrigerant side where it is: pressure switches, service valves, reversing valve, accumulator, filter drier, compressor and coil.
steps.warn: Never cut, drill, unbraze or heat a line. This loop holds kilograms of refrigerant and a cut line sprays liquid that freezes skin and eyes. Don't crimp it either: the valves are 3/4 or 7/8 in, and Yellow Jacket's pinch-off tool is rated for 1/4 to 1/2 in.

steps.text: If you want the steel, unscrew the louvre or guard panels from around the coil and lift them clear without dragging them across the fins or tubes.
steps.warn: Leave any panel that a tube, the coil or a valve is fixed to.

steps.text: With the panel breaker still off and tagged, take the pull-out block and any cartridge fuses from the disconnect. Take the whole box only if you know how to work on fixed wiring and the panel breaker stays off and tagged: prove its supply terminals dead (live, dead, live), undo the supply wires, cap and tape each one, and change the panel tag to: Wires cut and capped. Do not switch on.
steps.warn: Until the panel breaker is off, the supply terminals inside the box are live even with the block pulled out or the switch off.

notes:
## Two circuits, one big charge

- **Power.** Goodman warns that more than one power source may be present (Goodman IO-778B), and Carrier that there may be more than one disconnect switch, to be locked out and tagged (Carrier 24ACB-C-6SI). The indoor unit's transformer supplies the 24 V control power to the outdoor unit (Goodman IO-778B; Carrier 24ACB-C-6SI), so the thermostat being off proves nothing about the 240 V side.
- **Live while silent.** Goodman fits a 230 V, 40 W crankcase heater to its GSZ14 heat pumps and lists a one-pole, 24 V contactor (Goodman RP-G4002J), and says units with crankcase heaters should have power on for 24 hours before start-up (Goodman IO-778B). A quiet unit can still be live.
- **Capacitor voltage.** Friedrich's window-unit manual says that on a typical 230 V circuit the start terminal of a motor can see as high as about 400 V while it runs, and that many motor capacitors are internally fused, so shorting them ruins them: drain them through a resistor (Friedrich Q manual). That is a running voltage, not a measured stored charge, so treat every capacitor as live until the meter reads under 1 V. Goodman's GSZ140361 capacitor is rated 5/45 µF, 440 V (Goodman RP-G4002J).
- **Refrigerant.** Carrier says to relieve pressure and recover all refrigerant before repair or final disposal, and that federal rules forbid venting it (Carrier 24ACB-C-6SI). In the US, refrigerant from a central air conditioner or heat pump must be removed by an EPA-certified Type II or Universal technician with certified recovery equipment (EPA disaster guidance).
- **The charge can sit behind closed valves.** Outdoor units ship with their service valves closed to hold the charge inside, and the installer opens them at start-up (Goodman IO-778B; Carrier 24ACB-C-6SI). The sources don't say what state an installed unit's valves are in. If they are closed, the unit can still hold its whole charge after its line set is cut, so cut lines outside don't prove it is empty.
- **Why crimping doesn't apply.** The crimp-first method (teardown_fridge_compressor) is written for small fridge tubing. The suction valves here are 3/4–7/8 in (Goodman SS-GSZ14; Carrier 24ACC6 data), and the one bar-style pinch-off tool in Yellow Jacket's brochure is listed for 1/4 to 1/2 in copper (Yellow Jacket brochure). No source read shows a crimp holding at these sizes and charges, so don't try it. The 3-ton units hold 6.75 lb (3.06 kg) of R-410A (Carrier 24ACC6 data) or 115 oz (3.26 kg) (Goodman SS-GSZ14). Goodman also warns the scroll compressor's dome can be hot (Goodman IO-778B).

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Fan motor and blade.** Carrier's size-36 unit uses a direct-drive propeller fan moving 3,223 cfm on a 1/12 hp, 800 rpm motor (Carrier 24ACC6 data). Goodman's GSZ14 motors are 1/6 or 1/4 hp, 8-pole, single speed, some listed as PSC, and its larger sizes use a 26 in aluminium blade (Goodman RP-G4002J). With its capacitor's FAN section it makes a big exhaust or drying fan wherever 208/230 V power exists.
- **Dual run capacitor.** A spare for motors and compressors that call for the same values (test_capacitor).
- **Contactor.** A 24 V AC coil switching 25 A or 30 A (Goodman RP-G4002J). It can switch a pump or heater from a 24 V AC control circuit such as a furnace or doorbell transformer.
- **Hard-start kit.** A start capacitor and relay that give the compressor a boost at each start; Carrier sells one as an accessory (Carrier 24ACC6 data). A spare for a stubborn single-phase motor.
- **Disconnect and fuses.** The 3-ton units call for at most a 30 A time-delay fuse or breaker (Carrier 24ACC6 data), or 35 A in time-delay fuses or HACR-type breakers (Goodman SS-GSZ14). The box is a switch for a workshop or pump circuit: check its rating label before you use it outdoors.
- **Defrost board (heat pumps).** Goodman's is part PCBDM133 (Goodman RP-G4002J). Its relays and connectors are small spares.
- **Temperature sensors.** Clip-on thermistors for thermostat and monitoring builds.
- **Galvanised steel.** Goodman's cabinet is heavy-gauge galvanised steel with a steel louvre coil guard (Goodman SS-GSZ14): weather shields, heat shields, boxes.

## Testing what you got out

- **Fan motor.** Wire it as its label or the unit's diagram shows, with its capacitor, at its rated 208/230 V. Bench-test only through an RCD or GFCI, with the terminals covered and the blade off.
- **Contactor.** Put 24 V AC on the coil: it should pull in with a clunk. With the coil off, check the contacts on the ohms range: open; with it on, near 0 Ω.
- **Capacitor.** See test_capacitor; test both sections.

## Variations

- **Carrier 24ACC636 (cooling only).** Scroll compressor, R-410A, 7/8 in vapour valve; high and low pressure switches standard; crankcase heater and hard-start kit as accessories (Carrier 24ACC6 data).
- **Goodman GSZ140361 (heat pump).** Scroll compressor, 115 oz R-410A, 3/4 in suction valve, 173 lb (78 kg). It adds a reversing valve, an accumulator, a crankcase heater, a defrost board, and high and low pressure switches (Goodman SS-GSZ14; Goodman RP-G4002J).
- **Older units** may use R-22, and the newest may use a flammable refrigerant such as R-454B: Carrier's instructions for its R-454B outdoor unit call for non-sparking tools, no open flames or other ignition sources, and a recovery pump certified for flammable refrigerants (Carrier II146SAN). **Inverter-driven (variable-speed) units** may have an electronic drive board instead of a simple contactor; Carrier's service manual for its inverter ductless outdoor units says charge stays in the board's capacitors after the supply is shut off (Carrier 538PR). Treat those capacitors as a DC bus (see safety_discharge_capacitor) and check yours.

## What to leave

- The whole refrigerant side: compressor, outdoor coil, service valves, reversing valve, accumulator, drier, pressure switches and the line set to the house, plus the indoor coil at the furnace.
- Venting refrigerant, ever: it is illegal in the US and dangerous anywhere (EPA disaster guidance).
- Any panel that holds a tube or valve.
